subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: “Five minutes, Mummy, just five minutes!” Kishore called, crayon already moving over the paper. The school bus came at 7:40, and it was 7:25. His mother Swati kept an eye on the clock while she packed the tiffin. The sun took three minutes. Then the mountains needed a river, and the river needed a boat with a flag, and the flag needed all the colours. At 7:38 the bus honked. Kishore looked up, astonished. “Already?” he said, and meant it. He grabbed the drawing, still wet in the corners, stuffed his shoes on the wrong feet and ran down the stairs with the picture smudging against his shirt.

qa.q: What time did the school bus come?
Why was Kishore astonished when the bus honked?
qa.a: Kishore sincerely believed only five minutes had passed and felt surprised and a little shocked that the time had run out so soon.

qa.q: What could Kishore and Swati try tomorrow so the drawing does not collide with the bus?
qa.a: Set a timer for the drawing, or start earlier, and decide which part gets finished before the bus.

qa.q: How might Swati feel watching the clock while packing the tiffin?
qa.a: Swati is likely anxious about the bus and patient with Kishore at once, since the promise of “five minutes” was sincere but unreliable.

grounding: A child promises a drawing will take five minutes and is surprised by how much time has gone.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Tenzin sat on the sofa with a football in hand. “You said five minutes,” Tenzin said. Mridul didn't look up from his block castle. “Five minutes,” he agreed. The clock over the door said 4:10. Mridul added a bridge, then a tower, then a gate that opened. He was sure he had only just begun. At 5:05 Tenzin put the football down, said “I'll go down to the park with Kabir,” and left. Mridul glanced at the clock and frowned. “That was quick,” he said to the empty room. Through the window he could see two small figures on the grass, already kicking the ball, and the castle suddenly looked smaller.

qa.q: What time did the clock over the door show when Tenzin was waiting?
qa.a: The clock over the door said 4:10.

qa.q: What did Mridul feel when he saw the clock at 5:05?
qa.a: Mridul felt surprised and frowned, because to him the time seemed to have passed so quickly; his “That was quick” shows the promise of five minutes was sincere.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next time before promising Tenzin a time?
qa.a: Look at the clock when starting, guess how long the castle will really take, and tell Tenzin an honest time or stop at a set hour.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after waiting almost an hour?
qa.a: Tenzin is probably disappointed and a bit annoyed at waiting, yet still wants to play, so leaves for the park with Kabir.

grounding: A child promises five minutes and loses an hour, with little felt sense of duration.
